source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping (Exp 1, re-read in full)
finding: Exp 1: people judged which of two equally true target-matching facts supports an analogy. Facts embedded in a shared causal system won. A control group that read only the target showed no such preference, so the effect is not about fact importance.
numbers: N=48 undergraduates (Illinois), analogy vs target-only groups (df 44). Choice task: mean shared-system choices out of 4 passages 3.17 (analogy) vs 2.0 (target-only), F(1,44)=18.43, p<.001. Ratings: shared 6.28 vs different 4.89 (analogy); 5.22 vs 5.31 (target-only); condition x fact-type F(1,44)=13.99, p<.001. Per passage, analogy chose shared-system fact 67-92% vs 42-54% for controls; Fisher exact significant (one-tailed p<.05) for 3 of 4 passages.
quote: analogy subjects chose the shared-system fact 67% to 92% of the time
limits: Four passages only. Same lab and same materials family throughout. Both facts were true statements, so this tests selection, not truth.
agent_relevance: Supports a mapping scorer that credits a match more when it sits inside a connected relational system (O7). Our code can implement that credit as a number.

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Exp 2 (free prediction from the analogy, re-read in full)
finding: Exp 2: people predicted new facts about the target. They most often predicted the one that followed from the shared causal system, though both were possible. Resolves earlier conflict: Exp 2 has N=32 (16 per group).
numbers: N=32 (16 analogy, 16 target-only; df 28). Free prediction, proportion of responses: shared-system .53, different-system .12, other .27 (analogy); target-only .12, .12, .74. Shared minus different count: M=1.63 vs 0, F(1,28)=20.05, p<.001. Prediction ratings 6.03 vs 4.41 (analogy). Choice task M=2.9 vs 1.8, F(1,28)=16.43, p<.001. Judge agreement .88.
limits: Small N. One passage looked biased; results still held without it (F(1,28)=13.03, p<.001). Same lab as the theory.
agent_relevance: Free inference is steered by the system around a match, not only by local match. A candidate-inference step in O7 should rank inferences by the connected structure they extend.

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Exp 3 (base held in memory only, re-read in full)
finding: Exp 3: same task, but people memorised the base first and could not look back. The effect held but was weaker, and failed for one of three passages. Resolves earlier conflict: Exp 3 has N=48 (24 per group, df 44), not 46.
numbers: N=48 (24 vs 24). Shared minus different predictions: M=.92 (analogy) vs .13 (target-only), F(1,44)=5.15, p<.05. Choice: M=1.875 vs 1.0 out of 3, F(1,44)=13.15, p=.001. Table 8 overall rows were garbled in extraction and are not quoted; analogy group predicted the shared-system fact most often (.46, .375, .75 by passage). Passage 2 showed no effect (.54 vs .58 chose the shared fact); the other two passages .66 vs .08 and .33 (Fisher p=.001, p=.05).
limits: Authors tie the Passage 2 failure to poor memory of the base. One of three passages failed to show the effect, so the effect is not uniform. No independent-lab replication was found in this or earlier passes.
agent_relevance: Systematic selection weakens when the base is recalled imperfectly. For the agent: keep the base case text in view when mapping, do not map from a summary.

source: Gentner & Gentner (1983) Flowing waters or teeming crowds: mental models of electricity (chapter, full text)
finding: The empirical anchor for structure-mapping: the analogy people hold (water flow vs moving crowd) predicts which circuit problems they get right. Exp 1 worked as predicted; Exp 2 (taught models) worked only in part.
numbers: Exp 1: 36 students recruited; only subjects with consistent models kept: 7 fluid-flow, 8 moving-crowd (df 13). Model x Component interaction F(1,13)=4.53, p<.05; nothing else significant. Exp 2: N=18 (7 crowd, 6 pump, 5 reservoir). Parallel-resistor current, qualitative: crowd .93 vs .63 for the other two groups combined (chi-square p<.05); voltage .86 vs .42 (pump) and .50 (reservoir). The prediction that the reservoir group would excel at batteries failed (.40 R, .64 M, .33 P, ns).
quote: use of different analogies leads to systematic differences in the patterns of inferences
limits: Tiny analysed samples after screening on model use. Authors say Exp 2 was weaker partly because subjects did not understand water systems (base-domain scores .35 R, .42 P, .32 M). A mapping can only transfer structure that the reasoner actually holds.
agent_relevance: Mapping a bad or shallow base gives bad inferences. Before O7 transfers inferences, the agent should check that it holds the base relations correctly.

source: Gentner (1983) Structure-mapping: a theoretical framework for analogy (scanned PDF, re-attempted)
finding: Re-attempt on gap 8: the scanned PDF still gives text only for the last pages (discussion and references). It is a theory paper. The only empirical study tied to it that is readable is Gentner & Gentner (d04). No separate tables experiment could be confirmed.
numbers: Extracted text about 86 KB, almost all reference list and discussion. No experiment tables recovered.
limits: Gap 8 stays partly open: Gentner 1983 core text is not verified. Do not cite numbers from it. A page-image OCR copy is needed (no OCR tool on this machine).
agent_relevance: Cite Gentner 1983 for the rules (one-to-one, relations over attributes, systematicity) only, from later papers that restate them.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Lovett & Gentner (2017) Extending SME to handle large-scale cognitive modeling (re-checked)
finding: Confirms two numbers that were unverified: greedy merge matched exhaustive merge on 52 of 56 analogies (93%), and an SME visual-oddity model solved 39 of 45 problems; failures were among the hardest for humans.
numbers: 52/56 = 93% (greedy vs exhaustive, from Forbus & Oblinger 1990 test on a library of SME examples). 39/45 visual oddity problems.
limits: The greedy-merge test is the SME authors' own, on their own example library (not independent). The oddity model is a hand-built pipeline.
agent_relevance: A greedy scorer is a safe default for O7: it loses little against exhaustive search.

source: Weitekamp & MacLellan (2026) SMTB: fast structure-mapping with tight bounds (re-read)
finding: Correction: the speedup is 5-15x, not 515x (the earlier figure came from a lost en-dash). SMTB also finds better mappings on large nested problems, and the paper explains how SME's higher-order bias fails on flat or loosely matched representations.
numbers: 5845 domain pairs from the SME corpus. Whole-corpus time: SME 70.95 s; greedy SMTB 5.97 s; backtracking w=3,d=3 30.99 s; w=3,d=1 gives a steady 5-15x speedup. Score vs SME: +21.6% (L=0), +22.6% (L=3). Kernel-violation mappings fell from 9.16% to 5.84% in 'thermo' and 0.14% to 0.0% in 'moraldm' with paired walks. Abstract: about 50% better mappings in large nested domains.
quote: SME becomes equivalent to greedy merging over candidate expression pairs
limits: No noise or corruption experiment: robustness to noisy representations is argued by example (algebra 4x+1=32 vs 4x+1=9, where SME drops the shared Equal) and not measured. Evaluation is on the SME corpus, which is hand-built.
agent_relevance: Where the agent's relations are flat (plans, PDDL-like), a higher-order bias gives no signal and SME reduces to greedy matching. Use connectivity-based scoring, not nesting depth, if representations are flat.

source: Alfieri, Nokes-Malach & Schunn (2011/2013) Learning through case comparisons: a meta-analytic review (re-read, ERIC copy)
finding: Re-read confirms the headline: case comparison beats other study formats with a medium effect. The 0.5 vs 0.6 difference is level of analysis (tests vs experiments).
numbers: 57 experiments (336 tests), random effects: d=.60 (95% CI .47-.72) at experiment level; d=.50 at test level; I2=59.05. Near-transfer comparisons .52, far .34 (far CI .20-.48).
limits: Heterogeneous; includes studies of contrasting cases that are not strict structure mapping. Far-transfer effect is smaller.
agent_relevance: Use d about 0.5-0.6 for comparison prompts. Expect smaller gains for far transfer.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning (re-read)
finding: Permuted-alphabet letter strings with interval 2: plain GPT-4 is far worse than humans; GPT-4 with code execution matches humans. The model wrote the code itself, only to turn letters into positions. This is the nearest existing evidence that code-scored sub-steps remove procedural errors.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). Humans vs GPT-4: P=8.9e-13. Humans vs GPT-4+code: P=0.496 (no difference). Interval-size effect: humans P=1.5e-11, GPT-4 P<2e-16, GPT-4+code P=0.066 (not significant). 46% of GPT-4 errors follow a valid alternative rule (humans 39%). Same result on a new alphabet, and on an older engine with cutoff before the benchmark was public.
limits: One task family; GPT-4 era; code use not compared with a free-text arm at equal tokens; accuracies are in a figure, not a table. The code only does counting, not the mapping.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: not a direct test. It shows that deterministic code helps on the index/count part of mapping, which supports computing alignments in code.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) counterfactual letter-string study (raw-text re-check of Table 2)
finding: Row labels resolved by raw-text extraction: humans .753, GPT-3 .488, GPT-3.5 .350, GPT-4 .452. The order is read, not inferred. GPT-3 beats the later models on the counterfactual set.
numbers: Accuracy with 95% CI: humans 0.753 [.734,.773] (1,876 samples); GPT-3 0.488 [.467,.509]; GPT-3.5 0.350 [.330,.370]; GPT-4 0.452 [.431,.473] (6,840 samples per GPT model). The later version (2411.14215) reports humans .754 and says GPT-4-1106 and GPT-4-0125 were no better than GPT-4-0613.
limits: GPT-4 era only. Letter strings, not relational mapping of rich cases. CIs of the three GPT rows do not overlap, so the order GPT-3 > GPT-4 > GPT-3.5 is real in this sample.
agent_relevance: Closes the label caveat. Claim K09 numbers stand.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas & Mitchell (2025) Can large language models generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Letter-string analogies in Latin, Greek (near) and a symbol list (far). Adults and children transfer; LLMs lose much accuracy, most on the far symbol set.
limits: Models are 2024 releases (no reasoning models). Column order read from the table layout and the abstract (Greek near, Symbol far). Children's sample small.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 (partial): strong 2024 models still fail far transfer where children do not. Mapping must not depend on the surface token set.

source: Hellwig, Zuidema, Stevenson & Lewis (2026, COLM) Transformer See, Transformer Do: copying as an intermediate step in learning analogical reasoning
finding: Tests newer frontier models (GPT 5.2, Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-OSS 120B, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama) on letter-string analogies with permuted alphabets as a comparison for a small trained transformer. Frontier models still struggle on some transformations that are easy for humans. Exact frontier numbers are only in a figure.
numbers: Small 3-layer model: seen transformations on seen / new alphabets 96.7% / 93.9%; new transformations only 13.1% / 12.3% (mean of 10 runs). Best frontier LLM was GPT-OSS 120B. In few-shot (1-5 examples) results were mixed: Gemini 2.5 Flash and Llama 3.3 70B improved, GPT-OSS models got worse with 2 or more examples.
limits: Frontier bars are in a figure and could not be read as numbers. These are not o1/o3-class results with reasoning budgets stated. A train-from-scratch model is not our setting.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 (partial): no clean 2025-2026 reasoning-model score on the Lewis & Mitchell design was found. Adding examples can hurt strong models.

source: Chen, Wang & Wang (2026) ARCANA: a benchmark for abstraction and analogical reasoning
finding: Far-analogy mapping from real-world phenomena to grid transformations. Frontier 2026 models still sit well below humans. A Copycat-style prompting framework (ConceptSIR) with code execution solved some tasks that direct prompting missed.
numbers: Pass@3 union over 12 attempts, strict (-typo) / lenient (+typo): GPT 5.2 48.33/51.20%; Gemini 3 Pro 29.19/43.06%; Grok 4.1 Fast 18.66/24.88%; Claude Opus 4.5 7.18/8.61%. Humans pass@1 58.35/68.96%; tasks solved by at least 2 participants 93.5/96%. Language CoT only: GPT 5.2 38.28/40.19%. ConceptSIR solved 9 of 17 hard tasks, 2.22 loops on average.
limits: Reasoning effort left at default via OpenRouter; scoring done by hand; pass@3 union is a generous upper bound for models and pass@1 for humans. Authors say ConceptSIR is not general (code execution, error-driven mutation).
agent_relevance: Gap 3: best current evidence on frontier models and far analogy. A loop that proposes a mapping, checks it by code and revises can help, but the benchmark is not our permuted-relation design.

source: Khojasteh et al. (2026) YARN: LLM-derived abstractions for structural mapping of narratives (results and error analysis re-read)
finding: Structure mapping needs the LLM to extract and abstract events first. Without abstraction the mapping is below chance; with abstraction it beats LLM-only on far analogies and loses on near ones. Authors list extraction and abstraction errors but report no parse-accuracy figure.
numbers: MCQ: Qwen 0.17 without abstraction vs 0.46 with conceptual+evaluative (best LLM-only 0.41); Llama 0.16 to 0.45 (LLM-only 0.28). ARN, Qwen: YARN near 0.69 vs CoT 0.79; far 0.47 vs 0.52 (zero-shot). Llama far 0.46 vs 0.42. Asking for high-level message vs event mapping, Qwen zero-shot, ARN near: 0.88 vs 0.52. Far-near cases stayed below the 0.50 random line in all settings.
limits: Open-source models only (Qwen, Llama); event phrases compared by cosine over text embeddings. Error types are described, not counted. An NLI scorer gave 0.6 accuracy in a preliminary test.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the representation step is the weak link, but no number says how often the extracted structure is wrong. We would have to measure it ourselves.

source: Zeisler, Shirekar, Lica & Raman (2026) PRISM: category-theoretic framework for measuring and refining multimodal analogies
finding: Closest existing test of code-scored structure vs free-form choice. A code-computed relational score over VLM-extracted graphs picks the right analogy in 82.5% of AnaloBench items, below plain GPT-4.1 mini at 88.5%. The two make different errors. Removing the semantic-role step collapses the score to chance.
numbers: AnaloBench T1, 200 items, 4-way: zero-shot 88.5%; pullback score 82.5%, MRR .895, top-2 91.5%. Agreement: 159 both correct, 17 both wrong, 6 only score, 18 only zero-shot (McNemar p=.0227). Ablations: no chain bonus 76%; no semantic-role abstraction 24% (chance 25%). Human preference for refined images 57.65% of pairs.
limits: Not at equal tokens (the score pipeline needs graph-extraction calls). Small model as baseline. Single benchmark; the score is a validation step, not a claim to beat prompting.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a code-scored mapping did NOT beat free choice, but it is complementary (errors differ) and works only when role abstraction is right. Use it as a check, not as the sole judge.

source: Ye et al. (2024) AnaloBench: benchmarking the identification of abstract and long-context analogies
finding: Picking an analogy from 4 options is easy for short stories but falls with length. Retrieving analogous stories from a bank of 200 is close to random for long stories, even for the best model.
numbers: T1 accuracy at 1 / 10 / 30 sentences: GPT-4 89.1 / 66.5 / 60.7; Claude 68.2 / 30.2 / 25.9; GPT-3.5 65.3 / 46.4 / 30.8; Tulu2-70B 71.8 / 51.2 / 31.5; humans 96.0 / 72.5 / 73.3. T2 (retrieve top-k from a 200-story bank) near the random baseline for 10- and 30-sentence stories.
limits: GPT-4 and Claude-v2 (2023-24 models). Story lengths were stretched by GPT-4. No structure-first vs embedding retrieval arm. 2025-2026 models not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: no study found that compares structure-first retrieval with embeddings at equal tokens. Evidence that plain LLM retrieval of analogs from a large bank is weak.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Relevant or random: can LLMs truly perform analogical reasoning? (non-math tables re-read)
finding: Beyond math: self-generated relevant examples were below no examples on CommonsenseQA, MBPP code and GPQA with GPT-3.5, and below on GSM8K for four more models. They did help on BBH on average.
numbers: GPT-3.5 relevant vs none vs random-different: CSQA 70.8 / 73.4 / 72.9; MBPP 58.2 / 59.8 / 59.6; GPQA 31.6 / 34.4 / 33.1. GSM8K relevant vs none: Llama-2-70B 45.1 vs 51.4; Llama-3-8B 69.5 vs 72.3; Llama-3.1-8B 74.8 vs 77.3; Qwen2.5-14B 86.5 vs 89.1. Similarity of self-generated relevant examples to query: 0.46 (BBH), 0.48 (math).
limits: Largest model tested is GPT-3.5 or Qwen2.5-14B; no frontier or reasoning model. Examples were self-generated, not retrieved from a store. Self-generated examples may be wrong.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: for weaker models, relevant recalled analogs do not beat none or random off BBH. Whether this holds for strong reasoning models is untested. Do not claim analog recall helps without testing.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models as analogical reasoners (numbers re-checked against Chen et al.)
finding: Confirms the self-generated exemplar numbers used in the claims; gains are small on math. Chen et al. on the same two tasks found relevant self-generated examples scored lower.
numbers: Yasunaga self-generated exemplars: GSM8K 75.8, MATH 33.9 (GPT-3.5-turbo). Chen et al. relevant examples: 71.5 and 33.3 on the same tasks; no examples: 75.5 and 36.1.
limits: Different prompt wording; both use GPT-3.5. Not a failed replication of the same protocol.

source: Weitekamp & MacLellan (2026) SMTB: search for a noise-robustness figure (negative result)
finding: Searched the full text for a measured noise or corruption test: none exists. The robustness claim rests on three argued cases: no higher-order structure, notation-dependent nesting, and one failed lower-level kernel dropping all other correspondences.
numbers: Kernel-violation percentages are the only robustness-like numbers (0.14% to 9.16% across corpus domains at L=0).
limits: Gap 7 stays open: no figure of mapping score against percent of relations deleted, renamed or wrong.
agent_relevance: If we build O7, test our own scorer by deleting and corrupting a fixed share of relations; no published curve to rely on.
